title: blurb
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: From a tame horse pulling a chariot to the salaried musketeer that retired the knight — 4000 years of military dominance, none of it planned.

title: cart
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Domestication turned occasional drags into daily logistics; sledges exhausted people and animals until rolling bearings amortized the load.

title: horse
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: The cart already posed the question “what pulls this?” Horses were drafted into that existing vehicle economy—chariot warfare is cart-tech meeting a faster animal, not the invention of mounted combat.

title: bridle
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Charioteers could brace reins on the yoke; a solo rider has no third hand, so steering has to migrate to the mouth or control falls apart at speed.

title: saddle
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Mouth control answers direction; it does not absorb fighting shocks or spare the spine—without a weight spreader the mount fails before the rider does.

title: wooden-stirrup
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: A seat alone leaves the torso swimming sideways; hanging footholds buy the first real lateral purchase for archery—at the price of splintering under a melee hit.

title: metal-stirrup
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: The geometry was already right; wood was the weak link. Metallurgy is what lets the same loop survive the impact that proved leather and timber could not.

title: turnplow
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: This is not a detour: knight-weight mounts come from draft breeding, and draft breeding followed plow teams that could work northern clay—agrarian horsepower funds cavalry horsepower.

title: high-backed-saddle
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Stirrups fix side-to-side; a couched lance still punches you out the back—so the next failure mode is longitudinal recoil, not leverage.

title: iron-horseshoes
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Biomechanics solved, the bottleneck shifts to infrastructure: stone roads and campaigns grind hooves faster than unshod animals can sustain repeated charges.

title: couched-lance
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Shod, braced, cantled riders can finally spend the horse’s momentum budget on one pointed impulse instead of husbanding the animal’s feet.

title: horse-collar
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Shock cavalry is a calorie business; the collar is the farm-side multiplier that turns northern clay into surplus grain—and surplus grain into estates that can feed destriers.

title: longbow
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: The same centuries that perfected heavy cavalry also produced a weapon that ignores the contact zone entirely: plate and horse do not argue with yardage.

title: pike
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: If the knight’s advantage is reach at the gallop, answer with a longer static reach and cheap training—mass closes the distance economics against horse estates.

title: arquebus
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Close-order infantry was already normalized; chemical energy removes the decade-per-man skill curve and collapses the nobility monopoly on decisive shock.

title: standing-army
Rise and fall of heavy cavalry: Pike-and-shot is a payroll and drill problem, not a seasonal vassal obligation—the social contract that fed knights yields to the contract that feeds volleys.
